sonnet.problem: The story card right before it (card 3) already tells all of Job 28:3, saying the miner digs for ore in the deepest darkness and goes down there on purpose. That makes the false statement 'the darkness is too much for the miner' obvious. The question only re-asks what the previous card just told.
sonnet.rule: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

sonnet.problem: The question says no falcon has seen 'the miner's path', which tells the baker the animals don't know it. That rules out the wrong answers 'They hunt along it at night' and 'They guard the way down to it'. Calling it 'the miner's path' also adds a reading the text doesn't give, since v7 says only 'that path'.
sonnet.rule: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

sonnet.problem: The question asks what Job is 'showing about people' through the mining. Job 28:1-11 never says what the mining picture stands for. The right answer, 'They'll go to great lengths for hidden treasure', is the card's own interpretation, and the card is also a recap of the stop.
sonnet.rule: He retells the picture as the text gives it and says what it stands for only when the passage says so.

sonnet.problem: It asks the same point as card 5 (wisdom can't be bought with gold or silver) and card 2 (no one can know its value): no treasure measures up to wisdom. Card 5's answer already shows this, so 'None of them can compare to it' is a re-ask.
sonnet.rule: Two lines that make the same point get one question. An answer shown on one card, right or wrong, isn't used again on a later card.

sonnet.problem: The wrong answers 'The ocean told Him where it was' and 'He dug it up from the mountains' are not believable. Card 4 just showed the ocean saying wisdom isn't in it, and God needing to dig it up is silly. They make the right answer stand out.
sonnet.rule: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.
